title: The Market Ledger
body: Mama Bisi has sold pepper and tomatoes at Oja Oba market for twenty-two years. For most of that time she kept her accounts in her head. She knew who owed her, who paid on time and who always begged for 'small reduction'. Then, three years ago, her granddaughter Tolani gave her a cheap exercise book and taught her to write down every sale. At first Mama Bisi laughed. 'My memory is my bank,' she said. But after one month the book told a story her memory had hidden. On rainy days she sold far less, yet she still bought the same quantity of tomatoes from the farmers. Much of it rotted before Saturday. Now she checks the sky and the book before she buys. Her losses have dropped by almost half, and she has started saving for a freezer. Other traders laugh at the old woman with the exercise book, but many of them now ask Tolani for lessons too. Mama Bisi says the book did not make her clever; it only made her honest with herself.

title: Light After Six
body: When the solar lamps arrived at Ikere Community Secondary School, few people expected them to change much. The school had no grid electricity, and lessons ended with the sun. Students who lived far away walked home in the dusk and did their homework, if at all, by the weak flame of kerosene lanterns that filled their rooms with smoke. The lamps were small, each about the size of a mug, and they charged on the classroom roof during the day. Each evening, students could borrow one and return it the next morning. Within one term, the number of homework assignments submitted on time rose sharply. Teachers noticed fewer students sleeping in class, perhaps because they no longer had to wait for an older brother to finish with the family lantern. Parents mentioned something else: their houses smelt cleaner, and they were spending less on kerosene. The programme was not perfect. A few lamps were lost, and some families used them for business rather than study. Yet the principal insists that the experiment proved one simple point: when learning is made easier, students are willing to learn.

title: The Harmattan Visitor
body: Every year, between November and February, a dry wind blows from the Sahara Desert across West Africa. Nigerians call it the harmattan. It arrives quietly. One morning the sky is no longer blue but a pale, milky grey, and the sun looks like a dull coin. The air becomes dry and dusty. Lips crack, skin feels tight and furniture is covered in fine brown powder within hours. Mornings and nights are surprisingly cold, while afternoons can still be hot. For many people the harmattan is simply uncomfortable, but it can also be dangerous. The thick haze reduces visibility, so flights are sometimes delayed and road accidents increase. Dry grass catches fire easily. Doctors also report more cases of cough, catarrh and asthma attacks. Still, the season has its friends. Farmers use the dry weather to harvest and store grain, and many families enjoy the cool nights after months of heat. Like many visitors, the harmattan is welcome by some and dreaded by others.

title: Failing Forward
body: Chinedu failed his first attempt at the UTME by eleven marks. He spent a week refusing to leave his room, convinced that everyone in the street was talking about him. His uncle, a quiet engineer who rarely gave advice, finally knocked and sat on the edge of the bed. He did not say 'Don't worry'. Instead he asked to see the result slip and spent a long time studying it. Then he pointed out something Chinedu had ignored: his score in Physics was excellent, but his Use of English score had dragged everything down. 'You did not fail the whole exam,' the uncle said. 'You failed one part of it. That is much easier to fix.' Chinedu spent the next year reading a newspaper article every day and practising comprehension passages against a timer. He wrote down every unfamiliar word and its meaning in context. The following year he passed comfortably and gained admission to study engineering. He still keeps the old result slip in a drawer, not as a reminder of shame, he says, but as a map that showed him where to dig.

options.B: Studying failure carefully can show the way to success

'Dragged everything down' as used in the passage means

options.C: showed Chinedu exactly what he needed to improve

q.body: How did Chinedu improve his English?

options.B: By reading daily and timing his comprehension practice

title: The Okra Cooperative
body: For years, the okra farmers of Gidan Kwano worked alone. Each farmer carried a few baskets to the roadside, and each was forced to accept whatever price the traders from the city offered. Because okra spoils quickly, a farmer who refused a low price risked going home with nothing but a rotten load. In 2021, twelve farmers decided to try a different approach. They formed a cooperative, pooled their harvest and contributed money to rent a small cold room near the highway. Suddenly the balance of power shifted. With their okra kept fresh for several days, they no longer had to sell at sunset. They could also offer large, steady supplies, which attracted buyers from restaurants and supermarkets who paid better prices. The arrangement did not come without quarrels. Members argued about how to share profits and who should keep the key to the cold room. However, they wrote simple rules, elected a treasurer and held monthly meetings. Today the cooperative has forty members, and several young people who once planned to leave for the city have returned to farm.

title: Reading the Danfo
body: To a visitor, the yellow danfo buses of Lagos look like chaos on wheels. Conductors hang from open doors, shouting destinations in a rhythm that sounds almost musical, and drivers seem to obey no rule except speed. Yet anyone who studies the system for a while discovers an unwritten order beneath the noise. Each route has its own vocabulary: 'Oshodi-Oke', 'Obalende', 'CMS'. Passengers learn to read the conductor's hand signals, which tell them whether the bus is going straight or turning off. Fares change with the time of day, the weather and the traffic, and experienced commuters can predict these changes as reliably as an economist predicting inflation. Critics argue, with justification, that the danfo is unsafe and contributes to pollution, and the state government has introduced larger, regulated buses on several routes. Nonetheless, for millions of residents the danfo remains the most flexible way to move around the city. Its survival is a lesson in how people create informal systems to solve problems that formal planning has failed to address. Whether that is a triumph or an indictment depends on who is telling the story.

title: Grandfather's Radio
body: My grandfather's radio was older than my father. It was a wooden box with a cloth front and two round knobs, one for the volume and one that moved a thin red line across a row of station names. Nobody else was allowed to touch it. Every evening at seven, Grandfather sat on his low chair on the veranda, switched it on and waited for the news. While it warmed up, it hummed like a sleepy bee. We children learnt to keep quiet during those fifteen minutes, not because we were afraid of him, but because his face became so serious that the whole compound seemed to hold its breath. After the news he would explain what he had heard: why prices were rising, which country had a new president, what the weather would do to the farms. Years later, when I studied geography and economics, I realised how much I had already learnt on that veranda. Grandfather never went beyond primary school, yet he was the best-informed man in our village. The radio was his window on the world, and he generously opened it for us.

title: The Plastic Tide
body: Walk along almost any drainage channel in a Nigerian city after a heavy downpour and you will see the evidence: sachet-water bags, bottles and food packs piled against the bars of culverts like logs behind a dam. Plastic is convenient precisely because it is durable, but that same durability becomes a curse once it is discarded. A water sachet used for five minutes may survive for centuries. When drains are blocked, rainwater has nowhere to go, and streets turn into rivers that wash into homes and shops. Some cities have responded with bans on certain kinds of plastic packaging, but enforcement has been weak, and many small businesses insist they cannot afford alternatives. A more promising development may be the rise of collection schemes in which young entrepreneurs pay households for sorted plastic and sell it to recycling plants. These schemes turn waste into income and give people a reason to keep plastic out of the gutter. Their success, however, depends on the recycling plants paying fair prices and on residents believing that the extra effort is worthwhile. Technology alone cannot solve a problem that begins with human habit.
